ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
Detailed per-hectare production budget comparing corn grown without mulch versus with straw mulch applied (from a Kampong Cham-area trial, price basis $120/tonne):

Without mulch: yield 2.83 t/ha, giving revenue of $342.00/ha. Itemised costs include land preparation (disc plus harrow, about $63.65/ha total), basal KCl fertilizer (114 kg/ha at $0.34/kg, $38.76, plus application labour), planting and seed (60 kg/ha seed rate plus labour), urea top-dress (50 kg/ha at $0.32/kg, $16.00, plus application labour, $17.25/ha total), two rounds of hand-weeding ($18.75/ha each), and harvest/threshing labour ($25.00/ha). Total production cost was $323.31/ha, giving a net profit of $28.68/ha (note: this printed profit figure doesn't exactly equal revenue minus the stated cost, which would give roughly $18.69/ha -- reported as printed since the discrepancy could not be resolved from the source alone).

With mulch: yield 4.70 t/ha, giving revenue of $566.40/ha -- the same input costs as above, plus straw mulch spread at roughly 3 tonnes/ha at $18.00/tonne ($54.00/ha). Total production cost was $389.81/ha, giving a net profit of $176.59/ha (this figure does reconcile exactly with revenue minus cost).

Overall, adding mulch increased net profit roughly six-fold (from about $29/ha to about $177/ha) for an added direct cost of only about $54/ha, which is the basis for this source's recommendation that mulching is worth trying broadly where straw or crop residue is available. Farmers should treat the specific dollar figures as illustrative of the scale of benefit from this particular historical trial rather than as current prices or guaranteed costs.
